headline: Viking: low water on Europe’s rivers cuts occupancy and EPS misses, but 2027 bookings are 17% ahead and the shares rise 4%
takeaway: Revenue rose 9% to $2.18 billion on a bigger fleet, but historically low river levels pushed occupancy down to 91.3% from 96.0% and EPS of $1.11 missed the $1.26 consensus. Investors looked past it: advance bookings for 2027 are 17% higher than a year ago at 8% higher prices, and the shares rose 4%.
results: Viking Holdings reported revenue of $2,184.2 million for the third quarter, up 9.2%, as capacity measured in passenger cruise days rose 10.2% with new ships. Occupancy fell to 91.3% from 96.0% and net yield — revenue per passenger day after commissions and onboard costs — slipped 0.8% to $612. Adjusted gross margin rose 4.1% to $1,388.1 million.

Vessel operating expenses rose 17.6% to $461.4 million, mainly because of the larger fleet. Adjusted EBITDA fell 4.3% to $673.5 million and net income to $498.4 million from $514.0 million. Diluted and adjusted EPS were $1.11, against $1.15 and $1.20 a year earlier. Net leverage was 1.2 times EBITDA.

Historically low water levels on some European rivers disrupted parts of the river programme. Viking cancelled no scheduled cruises but used a range of mitigation measures to keep operating, and issued goodwill vouchers to affected guests.
mgmt: Chief executive Leah Talactac said fleet expansion, the diversified business and higher revenue per day supported strong revenue, and that nearly 30 years of experience on Europe’s waterways allowed the company to adapt to prolonged low water and minimise the impact on guests. She said demand remains resilient across the portfolio.

As of November 8, Viking had sold 93% of its 2026 core capacity and 68% of 2027. Advance bookings for 2026 were $6.2 billion, 11% above last year, though they declined since the previous report because of cancellations on disrupted itineraries. For 2027, advance bookings were $5.83 billion, 17% higher, at $929 per passenger day, 8% higher.
view: Viking’s model is unusual in cruising: it targets affluent travellers over 55, sells no casinos or children’s clubs, and books its capacity a year or more in advance at rising prices. That makes it more predictable than the mass-market lines, and it also means a weak quarter caused by weather tells you little about the next year. Low water on the Rhine and Danube is a recurring risk of river cruising — 2018 and 2022 were similar — and this summer’s drought hit occupancy and costs at the same time.

The bookings data is why the shares rose despite the miss. Having 68% of 2027 already sold, 17% more in dollars than at this point last year and at 8% higher prices per day, is an exceptionally strong position for a travel company. It means next year’s revenue is largely visible, with yield growth built in, and that customers who experienced disruptions are still coming back. Leverage of 1.2 times also leaves Viking with far more financial flexibility than Carnival, Royal Caribbean or Norwegian.

The structural question is climate. If low water becomes a regular summer feature, Viking will have to keep spending on mitigation, accept lower occupancy in some weeks and lean more on its ocean ships, which now drive most of the growth. The company’s scale on Europe’s rivers is a competitive advantage in normal years and a concentrated exposure in dry ones. At around 30 times trailing earnings, investors are paying for growth in the ocean fleet and pricing power; this quarter suggests both remain intact.
watch: Watch fourth-quarter occupancy as river levels recover, how many 2026 cancellations turn into 2027 rebookings, yield growth for 2027, and new-ship deliveries.
